Church year and calendar

Worship and practice · Church year

Church year and calendar

10 sectionsNot completed
Notes

The Church Year brings daily worship into relation with feasts, saints and seasons. A feast is a liturgical commemoration; these readings introduce the day’s beginning and the books used for changing service texts, with additional resources for the wider calendar.[1]

When does the liturgical day begin?[1]

Hapgood’s account begins the church day at sunset. Vespers, the evening service, consequently belongs to the opening of that cycle. The explanation connects evening worship with the expectation of Christ and the following Liturgy with the New Testament account of his saving work.[1]

Read original passage

Vigil and the church day

The Holy Orthodox-Catholic Apostolic Church of the East reckons its day after the pattern of the Jewish Church, from sunset. Therefore the worship of God begins with the Evening Service, which typifies, in general, the Old Testament times, as foreshadowing our Lord Jesus Christ and his life on earth, and precedes the Divine Liturgy of the morning, wherein is typified the life of our Lord as set forth in the New Testament and his life in heaven.

Which books supply the changing services?[1]

The Menaion contains services for the days and their saints and feasts. Hapgood also identifies the Pentecostarion with the Paschal season and the Triodion with Great Lent. These book names help explain why the words heard in church vary through the year.[1]

Read original passage

Services and feasts

(2) The Minéya is a set of twelve volumes containing the services for every day in the year, with the proper Hymns for the Saints of the day, and so forth. In addition, there are the Minéya of the Feasts, and the Pentecostáron (with the services for Easter-tide); and the Triódion, which contains the services, day by day, for the Great Fast.

What does the Annunciation commemorate?[5]

The Annunciation concerns Archangel Gabriel’s announcement to Mary of Christ’s birth, recorded in Luke 1. The linked OCA explanation relates the feast to the Incarnation, the Son of God becoming human.[5]

Source publication

Annunciation

Open source text

What does the Transfiguration commemorate?[6]

The Transfiguration concerns Christ’s revelation of his glory to St. Peter, St. James and St. John on the mountain. The linked OCA article connects that revelation with the apostles’ understanding of his approaching Passion and resurrection.[6]

Source publication

Transfiguration

Open source text

What does Dormition mean?[7]

Dormition means falling asleep and here concerns the death and glorification of Mary, the Theotokos or Mother of God. The article identifies Church Tradition as its source and notes that Mary’s death is not narrated in Scripture.[7]

Source publication

Dormition of the Theotokos

Open source text

What is the Elevation of the Cross?[8]

The linked OCA article explains the commemoration through the finding and later recovery of Christ’s Cross. It also relates the feast to Christ’s saving victory, distinguishing that theological meaning from its historical imperial associations.[8]

Source publication

Elevation of the Cross

This linked OCA resource concerns other feasts within the Church Year. It provides a place for further reading beyond the particular commemorations introduced in this lesson.[9]
